failure_modes: Assay sensitivity and low-biomass recovery failure: per-sample spike-in tracer and immuno-capture may not be recoverable or measurable from nasal lavage/CSF/olfactory mucosa levels, yielding artifactual absence of intact‑EV signal despite real differences in source material (false negatives).

Route/formulation/species clearance confounder: intranasal administration or species-specific barriers (mucus retention, rapid clearance) may prevent any detectable intact‑EV in short‑interval samples even for early‑passage/low‑p16/p21 materials, confounding attribution to senescence mechanism.

Non‑senescence upstream confounders: culture conditions, donor genetic variation, media composition, isolation/purification artifacts, or labeling effects could produce the observed orthogonal signatures independently of senescence mechanism, leading to incorrect causal attribution and inappropriate gating.

Spike‑in control failure: if exogenous intact‑EV tracer behaves differently from endogenous EVs (different capture efficiency or clearance) or is not validated across matrices, per‑sample recovery controls will be misleading, preventing interpretation.

Poor reproducibility and lot scarcity: requiring >=3 independent donor‑matched lots per senescence class may be infeasible or produce high inter‑lot variability unrelated to the tested senescence mechanism, making the gate unworkable and risking discarding clinically useful material.

Over‑interpretation risk: even if an analytic signature correlates with short‑interval recoverability in rodents, it may not predict clinically meaningful CNS delivery or potency in higher species or humans, so adopting a senescence gate could give false assurance of translational success.
strongest_objection: The most consequential bounded failure mode is that the orthogonal intact‑EV analytic + short‑interval intranasal recoverability paradigm cannot distinguish source-cell senescence effects from assay/administration/species limitations — i.e., either (A) the orthogonal assays and low‑biomass spike‑in controls lack the sensitivity/specificity required in nasal lavage/CSF/olfactory tissue (producing false negatives), or (B) intranasal delivery/formulation/species clearance prevents measurable intact‑EV exposure even for analytically 'favorable' lots. If either occurs, the study will incorrectly conclude senescence is non‑determinative (or will inappropriately gate lots), wasting resources and risking wrongful lot rejection.
